terms.definition: Google's deep-learning library; tf.data, Keras and the preprocessing layers of this chapter are parts of it.
TensorFlow's library for building input pipelines: read, transform, shuffle and batch data on its way to a model.
in this chapter, a tf.data.Dataset: a described stream of items that a model can read one batch at a time (not a table in memory).
TensorFlow's array: a number, a list, a table or a stack of tables, all of one type.
describe the work now, do it only when the result is asked for: a tf.data chain reads nothing until you loop over it.
a small group of items processed together; batch(7) packs 7 consecutive items into one tensor.
the computer's ordinary processor; in this chapter it prepares the data.
graphics processor: a chip that runs the model's arithmetic very fast; in this chapter it trains while the CPU prepares data.
one line of work a CPU runs; several threads run at the same time on several CPU cores.
a small holding area in memory where items wait between two steps.
tf.data.AUTOTUNE: let TensorFlow choose the number (of threads, of prefetched batches) from the machine it runs on.
the slowest step of a chain; it decides the speed of the whole chain.
prefetch(1): keep the next batch ready while the model trains on the current one.
put items in random order; shuffle(buffer_size) does it with a moving window of buffer_size items.
tf.reduce_sum(x): add up all the numbers in a tensor into one number.
TensorFlow's way of turning a Python function into a fast graph; map() needs functions it can convert.
one full pass over the training data.
the training method: nudge every weight a little in the direction that lowers the error, batch after batch.
independent and identically distributed: knowing one row tells you nothing about the next, and all rows come from the same population.
read several files at once and take one line from each in turn, so their lines are mixed.
the first line of a CSV file, holding the column names instead of data.
input/output: reading from and writing to disk or network.
a dataset that yields the lines of a text file, one line (as a byte string) per item.
how many files interleave() keeps open and reads from at the same time.
how many threads a step of the pipeline (such as map) may use at the same time.
raw bytes, shown by Python as b'...'; what a file line is before it is decoded into numbers.
tf.io.decode_csv: splits one CSV line on commas and returns one tensor per column, typed by record_defaults.
the list telling decode_csv each column's type and its fallback value; an empty tensor means the column is required.
a single number (a tensor with no dimensions).
glues several tensors of the same shape into one bigger tensor, e.g. 8 scalars into one vector of 8.
the declared structure of data: which fields, with which types.
training converges when it settles on good parameter values instead of bouncing around.
prepare raw data for the model: parse it, scale it, encode it.
cache(): keep the items in memory after the first pass, so later epochs skip reading and parsing them.
the share of time a piece of hardware is actually busy.
the part of TensorFlow for building and training models.
one step of a Keras model: it takes a tensor and gives back a transformed tensor.
Keras's simplest model: a plain list of layers, each feeding the next.
a layer in which every output is computed from every input by learned weights; Dense(1) outputs one number.
Keras's step that attaches the loss and the optimizer to a model before fit().
the number training makes small: how wrong the predictions are; "mse" = mean squared error.
the rule that turns each batch's error into weight changes; "sgd" (stochastic gradient descent) and "nadam" are two.
an object Keras calls at fixed moments of fit() (after each batch, each epoch) to do extra work.
compile() setting: how many batches fit() runs per call of its compiled training function (default 1).
using a trained model to predict (no learning).
TensorFlow's binary file format: a sequence of records, each any bytes, each guarded by checksums.
stored as raw bytes rather than readable text: smaller and faster to read, not human-readable.
a short number computed from some bytes; recompute it on read, and a mismatch means the bytes were damaged (CRC is one kind).
a common compression method: files get smaller, reading and writing cost a little CPU.
Google's format for structured data: a schema (.proto file) plus a compact binary encoding any language can read.
turn an object into a string of bytes you can store or send (parse: turn the bytes back into the object).
the protobuf compiler: turns a .proto schema into ready-made classes for your language (person_pb2.py for Python).
protobuf's name for a field that holds a list (email can hold several addresses).
the number each protobuf field gets in the schema (name = 1); the binary data stores the number, not the name.
wraps ordinary Python code so a tf.data pipeline can call it; slower, and the pipeline then needs Python to run.
tf.train.Example: TensorFlow's ready-made protobuf for one row: a dictionary of named features.
one named value of an Example; it holds exactly one of BytesList, FloatList or Int64List.
the three list types an Example feature can hold: bytes, floating-point numbers, or 64-bit integers.
storing a list of numbers as one run of bytes, without a tag in front of each number.
descriptions used when parsing: FixedLenFeature = always this many values (gives a dense tensor); VarLenFeature = any number (gives a sparse tensor).
a tensor that stores only the positions that hold values, with their values.
an ordinary tensor: a full rectangle of values.
a protobuf for rows that contain lists of lists: a flat context part plus named sequences (feature_lists).
a tensor whose rows may have different lengths, like sentences with different numbers of words.
the list of known words or categories, each with its own number.
training data prepared one way and production data another way, so the model receives inputs it was not trained on.
a Keras layer that standardizes each input column (mean 0, variance 1) with statistics it measures in adapt().
the method that lets a preprocessing layer look at data once and store what it needs (means, a vocabulary); no training.
a model made of layers; each layer's output is the next layer's input.
a Keras layer that turns a number into a bin index (which range it falls in).
one range of values; every value inside it gets the same index.
a distribution with more than one peak (two or three humps).
a Keras layer that turns category integers into 0/1 columns (one-hot, multi-hot) or counts.
a 0/1 vector with a 1 for every category present (one-hot has exactly one 1).
having a real order and spacing (1 < 2 < 3 with equal gaps); category IDs do not.
CategoryEncoding's setting: how many 0/1 columns (how many categories) there are.
a Keras layer that maps each text category to an integer index, most frequent first; unknown text gets the out-of-vocabulary index.
not in the vocabulary the layer learned (OOV); such values go to a reserved index, usually 0.
two different values that the hash function sends to the same bucket, so the model cannot tell them apart.
a small vector of learned numbers standing for one category (or word); similar ones end up close together.
having very many distinct values (e.g. 50,000 categories).
the pass that works out, for every weight, how much it contributed to the error, so gradient descent can adjust it.
a number a layer learns in training.
the model finding its own useful numbers for the inputs (e.g. embeddings) while it trains.
the small function a layer applies to its outputs (e.g. ReLU); "no activation" means the outputs pass unchanged.
a Keras layer that turns raw text into word indices (or TF-IDF weights): lowercase, strip punctuation, split, look up.
one unit of text, here one word.
filling short rows with 0s so every row of a batch has the same length.
term frequency x inverse document frequency: a word's count weighted down if it appears in many documents.
a text representation that keeps which words appear (and how often) but not their order.
one spelling with two meanings, like "bear".
a piece of a word ("evolution" + "ary"); subword tokenizers split words into such pieces.
a library and website of pretrained model parts you can download and use as a Keras layer.
already trained by someone else, ready to reuse.
one vector standing for a whole sentence.
a Keras layer that multiplies every pixel by scale and adds offset.
CenterCrop keeps a fixed-size rectangle from the middle of each image; Resizing changes an image's height and width.
randomly flipping, rotating or shifting training images so the model sees more variety; switched off outside training.
one dot of an image; here a number from 0 (dark) to 255 (bright).
a library that downloads standard datasets and returns them as tf.data datasets.
70,000 small greyscale images of handwritten digits 0-9, 28 x 28 pixels, the classic first image dataset.
tfds.load() setting that returns each item as an (input, label) pair instead of a dictionary.
an image set of 70,000 small grey photos of clothes, 28 x 28 pixels, in 10 classes such as T-shirt, trouser and ankle boot (60,000 for training, 10,000 for testing).
TensorFlow's web page of training charts (loss and accuracy per epoch) that can also show profiling data: where each training step spends its time.
the Large Movie Review Dataset: 50,000 film reviews from the Internet Movie Database (IMDb), each labelled positive or negative (25,000 to train on, 25,000 to test on).
the average of a review's word embeddings multiplied by the square root of its number of words (the book's exercise 10e; Chapter 16 explains why).
